extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of rhetoric/communication, media critics, and general readers interested in media/advertising analysis
extracted.subtask_description: A short academic rhetorical analysis that evaluates an advertisement (the Kendall Jenner Pepsi commercial) by applying rhetorical theory—especially kairos and ethos—to assess why the ad failed and how it misread its context and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kairos (appropriateness and timeliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kairos is a concept in rhetorical theory referencing appropriateness and timeliness; the opportune time to perform an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skilled rhetors capitalize on current events and public opinion to appeal to their audience. An ad must recognize whether it is an opportune time to engage a subject—airing a superficial commercial 'in the midst of Black Lives Matter protest prominence' was a severe misstep. Failed kairos includes trivializing traumatic events while the 'shock and pain caused by these tragedies remained fresh.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethos (credibility and trustworthiness of speaker/brand/celebrity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethos describes a speaker’s perceived credibility and trustworthiness; both PepsiCo and Kendall Jenner lacked adequate ethos to represent protests of this sort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the organization or spokesperson is an 'appropriate representative' for the topic. A snack/beverage company and a wealthy, uninvolved celebrity do not have the credibility to allude to complex political movements. Weak ethos undermines persuasive claims and can provoke backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of trivialization of serious issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads should not reduce or trivialize traumatic events or systemic injustices to simplistic gestures or marketing hooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commercial's premise—that handing a can of soda could 'rid the world of -isms'—was perceived as 'tone-deaf' and 'shallow.' Creators must avoid implying that grave social problems can be solved by a trivial product-based gesture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic representation of marginalized voices / avoid 'white savior' framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation must center the voices and experiences of marginalized people rather than using them as props or background to elevate a privileged actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting and narrative choices should not 'usurp the narrative' or 'centralize whiteness' so that people of color become props. Using a white celebrity as the focus of a protest about racial justice risks producing a 'white savior' effect and undermines message legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid co-opting social movements for profit ('piggybacking')
rubrics_metrics.description: Brands should not 'piggyback off of a movement that [they] were not affiliated with' or treat activism as a marketing trend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of motives; if an ad appears motivated by profit (e.g., 'trying to reach this generation' or make protesting seem 'trendy'), viewers will read the message as inauthentic. Watering down or broadening the protest to 'any protest movement' to avoid controversy signals opportunism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment between target audience and tactics/platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: An advertisement should correctly identify and address its target demographic and understand how that demographic communicates and judges media (e.g., millennials on Twitter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using platforms where the target audience expresses opinion (Twitter) can both inform strategy and reveal reception; misreading how that audience will react (tone, values, context) can magnify backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to contextual realities and risk factors (privilege and safety differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetors must recognize real-world risks and power dynamics—e.g., the differing safety implications for people of color approaching police versus a privileged celebrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portraying actions that are unrealistic or dangerous for marginalized groups (e.g., approaching armed police without consequence) exposes creators' ignorance of context and privilege, undermining credibility and inviting critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and specificity of visual/textual signs and messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagery and signage within an ad should convey clear, appropriate meaning rather than vague or generic slogans that dilute serious topics (e.g., signs that read only 'peace').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague visuals invite accusations of superficiality and make it easier for critics to juxtapose ad fantasy with real images of protest and brutality. Precise, contextualized imagery is necessary when handling charged subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rhetorical counter-evidence (effective critical response strategies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective critics use ethos and emotion-evoking visuals to demonstrate the juxtaposition between an ad's portrayal and reality (e.g., tweets pairing ad scenes with images of police brutality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating an ad's failure, consider how easily available counter-evidence (photos, news coverage) can be used by rhetors with high ethos to discredit the ad. The presence of such readily available refutations exacerbates a misread rhetorical situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and corrective response (apology and retraction as communicative outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misreading kairos and ethos can lead to swift public backlash, retraction of the ad, and corporate apology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the creator's post-release responses (defense, retraction, apology) acknowledge the rhetorical failures. A defensive statement that reiterates the same detached framing ('Live For Now') may further demonstrate lack of credibility; a prompt apology can be necessary after clear rhetorical missteps.
